source.title: Programming Refusal with Conditional Activation Steering

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the complete LessWrong post, described as a lighter version of an arXiv preprint. It includes references to figures, but the figures themselves and their numerical values are not present in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports the effect of standard activation addition with a refusal behavior vector on refusal rates, bearing on the addition part of V1, and compares it with conditional steering. It does not state that the tested vector was extracted by the original difference-in-means procedure. The rest of the post primarily uses refusal steering as a tool for conditional control.
record.gate_note: The standard activation-steering comparison reports that refusal rates increased indiscriminately across prompts. The post also reports CAST outcomes, which test conditional control rather than the claim versions; these are recorded with versions ["none"]. Dataset sizes used to construct training sets and choose thresholds are setup details, not result rows.
record.test_reason: The post uses a refusal behaviour vector as a tool for Conditional Activation Steering (CAST) and reports how well CAST works. Plain activation addition appears only as the comparator for CAST: its effect is described qualitatively, with no numbers, no stated difference-in-means recipe, no ablation and no capability check. The post does not set out to test whether one direction mediates refusal, so no verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. CAST selectively induces or suppresses refusal, composes rules, and constrains models to domains, with effectiveness tied to semantic distinctiveness. Conflicting suppression and induction rules can weaken induced refusal.
record.recipe_differences: The post applies activation addition with layer-specific behavior vectors and adds condition vectors plus thresholding to gate the behavior. It does not state that its behavior vector uses the original harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means recipe, and it does not test the original all-layer, all-position ablation. The post releases a toolkit implementation.
record.method_sensitivity: Condition-vector threshold, checking layer, and comparison direction are selected by grid search; behavior-vector layer and strength are manually searched. The text also reports that semantic distinctiveness affects domain-constraining effectiveness and that conflicting conditions can reduce induced-refusal effectiveness.

fits_no_version.finding: Gating the refusal vector by cosine similarity to a condition vector at a chosen layer raises refusal on harmful or chosen categories. Harmless refusal stays largely unchanged, across seven models (qualitative). Subtracting the vector removes refusal for selected categories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-vector steering can be applied conditionally, via separate condition vectors read from hidden states, to induce or suppress refusal for specific input categories.

record.problems: The supplied post omits the figures' numerical values and does not name the seven models in the general harmful/harmless evaluation. Most reported CAST outcomes are qualitative, and the text does not describe a general-capability evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified category-by-category values could be extracted because the referenced pie charts are not included in the supplied text. The text reports those category results collectively in r3 and r4. No other result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Extraction of the direction as harmful minus harmless difference-in-means; directional ablation; quantified refusal rates for addition; retention of general abilities.
All parts. The harmful condition vector is separate from the refusal behaviour vector, but the post does not test this as harmfulness encoding.

record.verdict_notes: The figures, and with them all numerical refusal rates, are absent from the post text. The seven models are not listed in the post; only Qwen 1.5 Chat 1.8B, Hermes 2 Pro and LLaMA 3.1 Inst are named. The full preprint (arXiv:2409.05907) may contain the numbers. Even so, standard addition is only a baseline there.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not state that its refusal vector was extracted as the harmful-minus-harmless difference in mean activations. It does not test ablating that vector, adding it as a single direction across every layer and position, or whether general abilities remain intact.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
No jailbreak attack is tested for suppressing a refusal direction, and no training against such ablation is tested.
The post does not test whether refusal is better described by an affine subspace, cone, or multiple directions.
No distinction between harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
No transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models is tested as a direction-transfer question.
No comparison of refusal training methods or training stages is made.

relation.reason: The refusal vector is the tool CAST gates. The post gives no result of its own on whether the single direction mediates refusal.

tranche.reason: The post builds on the refusal-direction finding and uses a refusal behaviour vector as a tool for CAST. It reports only CAST's performance. Plain addition is a comparator described in words only. The text states no difference-in-means recipe, no ablation and no capability measure.

source_check.notes: The post is a short version of arXiv 2409.05907 and gives no numbers. The seven models, the per-model rates and the behaviour-vector extraction recipe are only in the preprint or the figures. The text's dataset counts don't add up: 1,300 prompts per category, split 700 train / 500 test.
